title: The order of the day
hookLine: the day's verse is read from wherever the Granth falls open at the morning service

cards: Before dawn in Amritsar, once the Guru Granth Sahib has been brought into the Harmandir Sahib, the granthi opens the great book. Not at a bookmark or a chosen page, but wherever it falls open, and reads.
Whatever hymn comes up is the Guru's word for that day, and it travels far beyond Amritsar. Not a horoscope. Not a motivational quote on a poster.
A word for the day with weight to it, and chosen by no one.

teach.b: It's called the hukamnama. Hukam means command, order, the Divine Will: you met it in Japji, walk in the hukam. Nama means a letter, a written message.
So a hukamnama is a letter of command, a message from the Guru. The Sikh code of conduct describes how it's taken.

teach.h: THE TOP OF THE LEFT-HAND PAGE.
teach.b: When the Guru Granth Sahib is opened in the morning, the granthi opens it at random and reads the hymn at the top of the left-hand page, or, if that hymn began on the page before, goes back to its start.
That hymn is the day's hukamnama, sometimes simply called the vak, the word. It's often written up on a board so people can read it through the day.

Here's what's lovely: nobody chooses it. Not the granthi, not a committee, not you. Sikhs understand it as the Guru speaking to the sangat that day, and some take a line from it as their thought for the day.
The daily hukamnama from the Harmandir Sahib is shared around the world, online and on screens in gurdwaras from Birmingham to Vancouver, so Sikhs everywhere can start from the same word.
It's taken at other moments too: at a wedding, at a child's naming, before a big decision. A family may ask for one, and the first letter of the hymn often gives the new baby's name its first letter.
The word has a history outside the morning, too. The Gurus sent written hukamnamas as letters to distant sangats, and the Akal Takht still issues formal hukamnamas to the whole Sikh community.
Day to day, though, it's met here: a book falling open, and a word for today.

how: Each morning the Guru Granth Sahib is opened at random and the hymn at the top of the left-hand page is read as the day's hukamnama; the Harmandir Sahib's daily hukamnama is shared online for Sikhs everywhere.

practice: If you can, look up today's hukamnama from the Harmandir Sahib online; most sites give it in Gurmukhi with an English explanation, so read slowly and look for one line that seems to be speaking to you.
If you'd rather not look it up now, sit, ask yourself what you'd hope the day's one word for you would say, and listen to the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Hukamnama. A letter of command: the hymn read from wherever the Guru Granth Sahib falls open in the morning, the Guru's word for the day.
